title: canon verbs are a read-modify-write with no compare-and-swap, so two concurrent sessions on one thread silently lose a write
body:
## Summary

`Facade` canon verbs are a read-modify-write over a snapshot loaded at construction, with **no lock and no compare-and-swap**. Two concurrent CLI invocations touching the **same thread** silently lose the earlier write: no error, no conflict, and valid canon afterwards.

Reported by laksa-vc after laksa-ic's `at edit`/`green` erased a verified `ac edit` amendment on Laksa's ST0111. Mechanism re-verified here in this estate's source rather than accepted on report.

## Mechanism

`facade.rs:5215` is representative of the family:

```rust
let mut next = self.canon.clone();                      // whole in-memory snapshot
find_criterion_mut(&mut next, st, ac)?.text = text...;   // mutate one field
self.apply("ac.edit", ..., next)                         // write it back
```

`self.canon` is loaded when the `Facade` is built. Process A and process B each load, each mutate a **different** field, each `apply`. B's `next` is derived from B's stale snapshot, so it carries A's field at its **pre-edit** value and overwrites it.

**`apply_envelopes` narrows the blast radius but does not close the race.** It diffs `next` against `self.canon` and writes only threads that differ, so an edit to ST0056 cannot clobber ST0057. Within one thread the whole record is rewritten, which is where the loss happens. **The unit of the race is the THREAD.**

## Why it is worse than a hand-edit race

Hand-editing canon is documented as unsafe and people are told to use the CLI instead. **The CLI carries the identical race while feeling safe**, and this project ships the concurrency pattern that triggers it -- the whiteboard fleet is N sessions against one tree, and a thread like ST0056 is written by four nodes in an afternoon.

## The remedy is already in this function, applied to a narrower case

`apply_envelopes` carries a guard added after Lamplight lost 4934 bytes of issue prose, and its comment states the principle exactly:

> **Against the DISK rather than against `self.canon`, and that is the whole point.** `self.canon` is what this write is derived from, so comparing to it can only ever agree with itself. The file is the thing that loses the prose, so the file is what gets asked.

That is the shape this defect needs, scoped to one field (an authored body) instead of to the record. **The reasoning generalises verbatim and was not generalised.** Same shape as `whiteboard-clock-guard.sh`, which documented BSD's unspecified-field fill, fixed it for the decision-DATE path, and left the HH:MM path carrying the defect it described.

## Candidate remedies (not chosen)

- Re-read the thread from the store immediately before write and refuse if it moved since load (compare-and-swap on a revision or on the record hash).
- An advisory lock around the read-modify-write. Note `daemon.rs:957` already records that `flock` is unreliable over NFS and network home directories, so that route has a known caveat in this estate.
- Route canon writes through `intentd` when it is running, which serialises by construction -- the `--daemon` flag exists, but in-process is the default and the default is what races.

## What this does NOT claim

No lost write has been demonstrated in THIS repository. The mechanism is confirmed here by reading the source; the observed loss was on Laksa. A drive that plants two concurrent edits on one thread and shows one vanishing is the missing evidence, and it should be built before any fix is banked -- the fix must be shown to change a verdict the harness can produce.
